output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation reveals an amnestic profile with predominant involvement of verbal memory. Testing was administered in Spanish, her dominant language, with norms adjusted for age, education and language background. Episodic memory is disproportionately impaired: RAVLT delayed recall at the 6th percentile, immediate recall at the 12th percentile, and recognition at the 14th percentile, consistent with a storage-type deficit with poor benefit from recognition cues. Confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 22nd percentile) and semantic fluency (Animals, 19th percentile) are mildly reduced. Nonverbal memory (Rey Complex Figure delayed recall, 10th percentile) is also impaired. Processing speed, executive function, and visuoconstructive ability are within the low-normal range. Mood screening is within normal limits (Geriatric Depression Scale 3/15). Screening: MoCA 21/30, MMSE 28/30; the MMSE score falls within the conventional normal range. Profile is consistent with amnestic mild cognitive impairment.

output.interpretation: Opening pressure 15 cmH2O. Acellular CSF (WBC 1 cell/uL, no red cells) with normal protein (38.4 mg/dL) and glucose (66.0 mg/dL, CSF/serum ratio 0.61). Decreased Abeta42 and Abeta42/40 ratio (0.053) with elevated p-tau181 (68 pg/mL); total tau at the upper limit of the reference range (398 pg/mL): amyloid-positive, p-tau-positive biomarker profile of Alzheimer-type pathology. Clinical correlation recommended.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 21/30 despite MMSE 28/30, delayed recall not helped by a categorical cue, informant-confirmed decline over ten months, and preserved instrumental independence with self-compensated lapses, placing the syndrome at the MCI stage
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive assessment with informant history and functional staging
action_criteria.rationale: A normal primary-care MMSE did not settle her husband's concern; a more sensitive instrument and an explicit account of daily function are needed to document the decline and stage it [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amnestic profile with a storage-type deficit: RAVLT delayed recall at the 6th percentile with poor recognition benefit; MoCA 21/30 with MMSE 28/30, so the MoCA reveals impairment the MMSE misses
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile, resolve the discrepancy between MMSE and clinical concern, and establish a baseline
action_criteria.rationale: Formal testing with norms for her language and education resolves the gap between a normal MMSE and the informant's concern and sets a baseline for serial reassessment [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Reversible mimics excluded; TSH, B12, and folate within normal limits; mild hyperglycemia consistent with known diabetes
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid disease, B12 deficiency and metabolic derangement are treatable contributors and must be screened before the decline is attributed to a neurodegenerative cause [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild bilateral hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA grade 1-2) with borderline temporoparietal cortical volume loss; minimal small vessel disease
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with the dementia (volumetric) protocol
action_criteria.rationale: MRI grades medial temporal atrophy and excludes vascular lesions, hydrocephalus and mass lesions as causes of her decline [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not dismiss the cognitive complaints solely on the basis of a normal MMSE score without further evaluation
Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine as routine treatment for mild cognitive impairment; neither is approved for MCI and the guideline does not support routine use [AAN_dementia_2018]
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from a close informant; the patient's own report may underestimate the degree of change

Arrange cognitive and functional reassessment in 6 to 12 months and recommend regular exercise (at least twice weekly; she stopped her Zumba class four months ago); explain that no medicine is approved for mild cognitive impairment [AAN_dementia_2018]
Manage vascular risk factors: keep blood pressure (132/78) and lipids treated and HbA1c (7.0%) at target without hypoglycemia
Disclose the diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment, explain the risk of progression and what reassessment will look for, and discuss advance planning while she has full capacity
Review safety at each visit (driving, finances, medicines), which she currently manages independently, so that a change in function is detected early

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET]

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is not part of the MCI work-up; she has no seizures, episodic confusion or rapid progression
ECG does not contribute to the MCI work-up; her pulse is regular at 71, she has no syncope or palpitations, and no cholinesterase inhibitor is planned at this stage
Echocardiography is not indicated; there are no infarcts on MRI, no murmur and no heart failure
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; there is no syncope, palpitations or episodic event
Brain MRI with volumetric protocol is available and tolerated; head CT is inferior for assessing hippocampal atrophy

differential.key_features: Forgetfulness limited to isolated events is expected with aging, but a MoCA of 21/30 and an amnestic neuropsychological profile with impaired recognition exceed normal aging
Geriatric Depression Scale 3/15 is within normal range and she denies sadness, anhedonia or neurovegetative symptoms; a storage-type recall deficit is not characteristic of an affective presentation

differential.diagnosis: Mild dementia due to Alzheimer disease (staging alternative)
differential.key_features: Excluded at this visit by preserved instrumental independence: she still manages finances, medicines, cooking and driving, and her lapses are self-compensated
No visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuations or REM sleep behavior disorder
Lisinopril, atorvastatin, metformin, calcium with vitamin D and as-needed omeprazole carry no anticholinergic or sedative burden and cannot account for a progressive amnestic profile

key_clinical_evidence: The MMSE has a ceiling effect in people with higher education; a score of 28/30 does not exclude MCI, and a MoCA of 21/30 with an amnestic neuropsychological profile resolves the tension in favor of impairment

The neuropsychological profile (storage-type episodic memory deficit with RAVLT delayed recall at the 6th percentile and poor recognition benefit, mild anomia and reduced semantic fluency) is the typical amnestic pattern of MCI due to Alzheimer disease

Cholinesterase inhibitors are not approved for mild cognitive impairment and are not recommended routinely at this stage; serial assessment and vascular risk management are the evidence-based steps [AAN_dementia_2018]
In a Spanish-dominant bilingual patient, testing in the dominant language with appropriate norms is needed to avoid over- or under-diagnosing impairment on language-loaded subtests

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The MMSE is insensitive for early MCI, especially in individuals with higher premorbid education such as this retired teacher; the MoCA 21/30 and formal neuropsychological testing demonstrating a storage-type amnestic profile are the clinically actionable findings
red_herrings.data_point: MMSE 28/30, within the conventional normal range (24-30)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Agent concludes cognition is intact and halts or deprioritizes further evaluation, as the referring primary care provider did, missing the abnormal MoCA and amnestic neuropsychological profile

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect and herniation risk in older patients
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.

findings.result: Alert; oriented to person, place, year and month; gives the date as five days early.
MMSE 28/30: one point lost on orientation (date) and one on delayed recall (2/3 words recalled freely; the third not retrieved with a categorical cue). Clock drawing correct.
MoCA 21/30: delayed recall 1/5, mild imprecision on the cube copy and a trail-making error, difficulty naming the rhinoceros, letter fluency 10 words in one minute.
Fluent in English and Spanish with occasional word-finding pauses and circumlocution in English; comprehension and repetition intact; follows three-step commands.

Her husband reports ten months of repeated questions about same-day conversations, forgotten appointments despite her phone calendar, misplaced glasses, missed items despite a shopping list, slower reading of Spanish novels, and abandoned knitting projects.

Still manages the household finances, her own medicines and meal preparation, and drives familiar routes without incident; lapses are compensated by her calendar and lists, and no task has been taken over.

clinical_assessment.impression: MMSE 28/30 and MoCA 21/30, with impairment in delayed recall (MoCA 1/5), executive and visuospatial items, naming and verbal fluency. The third MMSE word was not retrieved with a categorical cue. Her husband reports decline over ten months in memory for recent conversations and appointments. Instrumental independence is preserved: she manages finances, medicines, cooking and driving, compensating isolated lapses with her own calendar and lists; the syndrome is at the mild cognitive impairment stage.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, validated neuropsychological testing, the cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI. Optional: amyloid status by CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET (one conclusive test). No drug-interaction step: no medicine is started for MCI.
key_educational_points: Normal MMSE does not exclude early MCI-AD; MoCA is the more sensitive instrument and should be used when clinical concern persists
The defining neuropsychological signature of MCI-AD is a storage-type episodic memory deficit with rapid forgetting and limited cueing benefit
Cultural and linguistic background should be considered when interpreting neuropsychological test results in bilingual patients
Informant report is an essential clinical tool; discrepancy between patient-reported intact function and informant-observed IADL decline is itself a diagnostic signal
No medicine is approved for mild cognitive impairment; serial assessment, exercise and vascular risk management are the evidence-based steps

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Elena Vargas is a 69-year-old right-handed bilingual retired elementary school teacher who presents to the outpatient neurology clinic accompanied by her husband, Roberto, for evaluation of gradually worsening memory and word-finding concerns. Her husband first became aware of the changes approximately ten months ago when he noticed she had begun repeating questions during conversations that had occurred earlier the same day — asking twice, for example, whether their daughter was planning to call that evening. Initially he attributed this to fatigue or stress. Over subsequent months, he observed that she sometimes forgot appointments that had been clearly discussed and entered in her phone calendar, something he says was uncharacteristic of a woman who had spent decades organizing an elementary school classroom. On three occasions she mislaid her reading glasses and spent considerable time searching for them before finding them in unusual places. Her husband noticed that her grocery shopping has become less reliable; she occasionally returns home without items on a written list she carried with her. He also reports that she has become noticeably slower at reading Spanish-language novels, stopping more frequently and sometimes re-reading the same paragraph — she herself has commented that 'the words don't stick.' She continues to manage household finances, drive on familiar routes without incident, prepare meals, and care for herself independently in all activities of daily living including bathing, dressing, and medication management. The lapses have had no lasting consequences: she compensates with her phone calendar and written lists, and her husband has not taken over or begun supervising any household task. Her daughters have not observed any personality change or mood disturbance beyond mild frustration when she notices a memory lapse. She denies persistent sadness, tearfulness, anhedonia, or neurovegetative symptoms of depression. Sleep is described as restorative by both herself and her husband; there are no reports of acting out dreams, excessive daytime sleepiness, or witnessed apneic episodes. She denies hallucinations, paranoid ideation, or behavioral changes. There have been no falls, seizures, tremor, or incontinence. Her appetite is unchanged and her weight has been stable. She was seen by her primary care physician six weeks ago, who administered an MMSE that scored 28/30. The physician reassured her and her husband that the score was in the normal range, but given the persistence of the complaints and the informant report, referred her to neurology. Mrs. Vargas herself says 'I know something is off — I was never like this with my students.'

neurological_exam.additional: No paratonic rigidity. No grasp reflex. No myoclonus. No signs of parkinsonism. Smell not formally tested.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing normal bilaterally. No dysmetria. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus or diplopia. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial sensation intact to light touch V1-V3 bilaterally. Face symmetric at rest and with activation. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal base and stride length. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. Rises from chair without use of arms.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and year; knows the month correctly but gives the date as five days earlier than today. MMSE 28/30: lost one point on orientation (day of the month) and one point on delayed recall (recalled 2/3 words freely at 5 minutes; the third was not retrieved with a categorical cue). Clock drawing is correct — numbers evenly placed and hands accurately set to ten past eleven. MoCA 21/30: deficits in delayed recall (1/5 words), visuospatial/executive (mild imprecision on the cube copy and a trail-making error), naming (difficulty with rhinoceros), and verbal fluency (10 words in one minute). Language is fluent in both English and Spanish; occasional word-finding pauses in English with circumlocution. Comprehension intact for conversational language and two-step commands. Repetition intact. Able to follow three-step command.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone in all extremities. No rigidity or cogwheeling. Strength 5/5 throughout. No pronator drift. No tremor or involuntary movements.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, and patellar tendons bilaterally. Achilles reflexes 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffman sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and temperature intact in all extremities. Vibration sense mildly reduced at bilateral great toes, symmetrical and age-appropriate. Proprioception intact at toes bilaterally.
